A butterfly is a 4-cycle, two shoppers who both bought the same two products: ann and bob with tea and jam, and bob and cy with jam and oat. Nodes are shaded by how many butterflies they belong to; bob and jam, in the accent color, are in both and count 2, every other node counts 1." width="100%"} A *butterfly* is a complete bipartite $K_{2,2}$: two nodes on each side with all four edges between them, which is a 4-cycle. It is the bipartite counterpart of a triangle (a bipartite graph has no triangles), so butterfly counts play the role that triangle counts play in clustering coefficients: two customers who both bought the same two products, or two authors who both wrote for the same two venues, form one. They are the squares counted by `robins_alexander_clustering()`, broken down per node. Each butterfly is counted once at each of its four nodes, so the values sum to four times the number of butterflies. On a graph that is not bipartite every 4-cycle is counted the same way (bipartiteness is not checked). Parallel edges count once and self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional nodes (IDs or labels) to report. If `None` (default), all nodes. The count always uses the whole graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node ID to the number of butterflies containing it. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, or a node does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Uses the vertex-priority wedge counting of Wang et al. (2019): nodes are ranked by degree, and each 4-cycle is found exactly once from its highest-ranked node $u$ as two wedges $u - v - w$ that share the opposite node $w$, with both middle nodes and $w$ ranked below $u$. A pair $(u, w)$ with $k$ such wedges closes $\binom{k}{2}$ butterflies, and each wedge's middle node belongs to $k - 1$ of them. This takes $O(\sum_{(u, v)} \min(d_u, d_v))$ time, far less than enumerating cycles. Results match NetworkX's `bipartite.butterflies()`, which counts the same way (and also ignores bipartiteness). ## Examples {.doc-examples} Three customers and three products: Ann and Bob both bought tea and jam, and Bob and Cy both bought jam and oats, so there are two butterflies, both through Bob and jam: ::: {#5111d24a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["ann", "bob", "cy", "tea", "jam", "oat"]) g.add_edges( [("ann", "tea"), ("ann", "jam"), ("bob", "tea"), ("bob", "jam"), ("bob", "oat"), ("cy", "oat"), ("cy", "jam")] ) {g.get_label_from_id(n): c for n, c in g.butterflies().items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'ann': 1, 'bob': 2, 'cy': 1, 'tea': 1, 'jam': 2, 'oat': 1} ``` ::: ::: In a complete bipartite $K_{3,3}$ every pair from one side and pair from the other form a butterfly, nine in all, and each node is in six of them: ::: {#9abf0a2e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} k33 = ec.Graph().add_complete_bipartite_graph(3, 3) counts = k33.butterflies() counts, sum(counts.values()) // 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ({1: 6, 2: 6, 3: 6, 4: 6, 5: 6, 6: 6}, 9) ``` ::: :::
